Minerals and their biological roles
Proteins and enzymes: structure, types and biological role

summary: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; glucose is an aldohexose, fructose a ketohexose, ribulose a ketopentose.
Sucrose (glucose + fructose, α-1 → β-2) is non-reducing; maltose, lactose and cellobiose are reducing.
Starch (amylose + amylopectin) and glycogen are α-glucose stores with α-1,4 chains and α-1,6 branches; cellulose is β-1,4 glucose; chitin is β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine; inulin is a fructose polymer.
A triglyceride is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three water molecules lost); lipids give about 39 kJ g⁻¹, more than twice carbohydrate.
Phospholipids are amphipathic and form membrane bilayers; steroids have four fused rings; waxes are esters of long-chain alcohols.

Seventeen elements are essential; Mg is in chlorophyll, Mo in nitrogenase, Mn and Cl split water, Ca forms calcium pectate, Zn is needed for auxin; mobile N, P, K, Mg show deficiency in old leaves first.

Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (n − 1 for n residues); secondary structure is held by H-bonds, tertiary adds ionic, disulphide and hydrophobic bonds, quaternary needs two or more chains.
Enzymes lower activation energy; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor; the induced-fit model (Koshland) replaced lock-and-key (Fischer).

sections.title: Classification systems, taxonomic hierarchy and binomial nomenclature

summary: Linnaeus (1758) gave two kingdoms; Whittaker (1969) gave five — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — chiefly on cell structure, body organisation and mode of nutrition; Woese (1990) placed three domains — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya — above them, on rRNA sequences.
The hierarchy runs kingdom, division, class, order (-ales), family (-aceae), genus, species; species is the basic unit.
Binomial names (Linnaeus, 1753): Latin, genus capitalised, epithet small, italicised or underlined separately; tautonyms are not allowed in plants.
Bacteria have a peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes, a nucleoid and often plasmids; they are cocci, bacilli, vibrios or spirilla.
Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan and stay violet; Gram-negative walls are thin with an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane and stain pink.
Bacteria are photoautotrophic (anoxygenic, except cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophic (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic.
Binary fission doubles the population each generation (N = N0 × 2^n); the growth curve has lag, log, stationary and decline phases.
Cyanobacteria are oxygenic prokaryotes with chlorophyll a and phycobilins, cyanophycean starch, heterocysts for N₂ fixation, and no flagella or sexual reproduction.

summary: Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs with chitin walls and glycogen and oil as food; their sexual cycle is plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis.

Phycomycetes have coenocytic hyphae and zygospores or oospores; Ascomycetes form 8 endogenous ascospores in an ascus; Basidiomycetes form 4 exogenous basidiospores on a basidium; Deuteromycetes have no known sexual stage.
Phytophthora (late blight), Albugo (white rust), Claviceps (ergot), Puccinia (rust), Ustilago (smut), Alternaria (early blight) and Colletotrichum (red rot) are the classic disease fungi.
Yeast is a unicellular ascomycete that buds, ferments sugar with zymase to ethanol and CO₂, and forms 4 ascospores; its cycle is haplo-diplontic.
Mucor has a coenocytic mycelium without rhizoids, sporangia with a columella, heterothallic conjugation and a zygospore that is its only diploid stage.
A lichen is a fungus (mycobiont) living with an alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont); its forms are crustose, foliose and fruticose, and it spreads by soredia and isidia.
Lichens are pioneers on bare rock and sensitive indicators of SO₂ pollution.

Green algae store starch and have chl a, b; brown algae store laminarin and mannitol and have fucoxanthin and algin; red algae store floridean starch, have phycoerythrin and agar, and never have flagella.

summary: Bryophytes are non-vascular embryophytes with a dominant haploid gametophyte and a dependent diploid sporophyte; water is needed for their biflagellate sperm.

Liverworts (thalloid, unicellular rhizoids, scales, elaters), hornworts (horn-like capsule, one chloroplast per cell) and mosses (leafy, multicellular rhizoids, protonema, peristome) are the three classes.

Marchantia is a dioecious, dichotomous thallus with barrel-shaped air pores and gemma cups; it bears stalked antheridiophores and archegoniophores; its capsule holds haploid spores and diploid elaters.
Pteridophytes are the first vascular plants; their dominant sporophyte has roots, stems and leaves; most are homosporous, but Selaginella, Marsilea, Salvinia and Azolla are heterosporous.

Dryopteris has a rhizome with ramenta, circinate fronds, and sori with a reniform indusium; its sporangium opens by the annulus; the spore grows into a free-living, heart-shaped, protandrous prothallus; sperm are multiflagellate.
Gymnosperms bear naked ovules, are wind-pollinated, have a haploid endosperm formed before fertilisation and no double fertilisation, and lack vessels and fruits.

Pinus is monoecious with long and dwarf shoots, needles in fascicles, winged pollen, and two ovules on each ovuliferous scale; fertilisation follows pollination by about a year; polyembryony is common.
A Pinus seed holds three generations: seed coat 2n, endosperm n, embryo 2n.

summary: A modified organ is identified by its origin, not its looks: nodes, buds or scale leaves mean stem (potato, ginger, onion, Colocasia, Opuntia pad, Asparagus cladode, Citrus thorn); sweet potato, carrot and radish are roots; pea tendrils and Opuntia spines are leaves.

Racemose inflorescences grow on and open acropetally; cymose ones end in a flower and open basipetally; tulasi has a verticillaster, Euphorbia a cyathium, the fig a hypanthodium and the sunflower a capitulum.

Flower terms the paper uses: actinomorphic or zygomorphic; hypo-, peri- or epigynous; valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary aestivation; monadelphous, diadelphous, syngenesious, epipetalous, tetradynamous and didynamous stamens.
Placentation is marginal (pea), axile (tomato, lily), parietal (mustard), free central (Dianthus) or basal (sunflower).
Fruits are simple, aggregate (many free carpels of one flower) or composite (a whole inflorescence); false fruits such as the apple include the thalamus.

Brassicaceae: Ebr ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G₍₂₎, siliqua. Fabaceae: Br % ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G₁, legume. Solanaceae: ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎ with epipetalous stamens and an oblique ovary, berry. Liliaceae: Br ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎, capsule.

Every group matters in Nepal: nitrogen-fixing bacteria and blue-green algae, gundruk and kinema, mushrooms and yeast, agar, Sphagnum, Azolla, pine resin and timber, taxol, lokta paper and sal timber — and the harm done by plant viruses, late blight, aflatoxin, poisonous mushrooms and invasive weeds.

The five named medicinal plants: neem (Azadirachta indica, azadirachtin), sarpagandha (Rauwolfia serpentina, reserpine, roots), yarsagumba (Ophiocordyceps sinensis, an ascomycete on ghost-moth larvae, cordycepin), tulasi (Ocimum sanctum, eugenol, leaves) and ginger (Zingiber officinale, rhizome, gingerols).

summary: An ecosystem has a structure (abiotic factors plus producers, consumers and decomposers) and a function (productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling).
A pond is zoned into littoral, limnetic, profundal and benthic; a forest is layered from canopy to litter.
Energy flow is unidirectional and follows Lindeman's 10 % law, so food chains are short; the energy pyramid is always upright while number and biomass pyramids can invert.
Decomposers work at every trophic level and form a detrital pathway, not the apex of the pyramid.
The six interactions: mutualism (+ +), commensalism (+ 0), parasitism (+ −), predation (+ −), competition (− −), amensalism (0 −).
In the nitrogen cycle Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Clostridium and Anabaena fix N₂; Nitrosomonas makes nitrite; Nitrobacter makes nitrate; Pseudomonas and Clostridium denitrify.
Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared; doubling CO₂ forces the climate by 3.71 W m⁻². Acid rain (pH below 5) comes from SO₂ and NOₓ; ozone loss is a chlorine-catalysed chain started by CFCs.

Nepal runs from tropical sal below 1 000 m through subtropical chir pine, temperate oak and subalpine fir to alpine cushion plants; the four named invaders are Lantana, Mikania, water hyacinth and Parthenium.

topics: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; the cell theory

sections.title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; the cell theory
The cell wall, the membrane and the organelles
The cell cycle; amitosis, mitosis and meiosis

summary: The cell theory (Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Virchow 1855) has exceptions: viruses are acellular and coenocytic hyphae are multinucleate without cross walls.
Prokaryotes have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, 70S ribosomes, a peptidoglycan wall and binary fission; eukaryotes have a nucleus, 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes and mitosis.
The plant wall is middle lamella (calcium pectate), primary wall (cellulose) and secondary wall (cellulose plus lignin); plasmodesmata connect neighbouring cells.
The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic of phospholipid bilayer and proteins (Singer and Nicolson, 1972), selectively permeable.
Mitochondria (cristae) and chloroplasts (grana, thylakoids, stroma) are double-membraned and semi-autonomous, with their own DNA and 70S ribosomes; chlorophyll sits in the thylakoid membrane.
Lysosomes are single-membraned bags of acid hydrolases — the "suicidal bags"; the Golgi packages and secretes and forms the cell plate.
Chromatin is DNA wound round histone octamers into nucleosomes; a replicated chromosome has two chromatids joined at the centromere, with telomeres at the ends.
Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are 9+2 microtubules moved by dynein and ATP; bacterial flagella are flagellin and rotate.

units.title: Molecular Genetics: DNA, RNA and the Genetic Code
topics: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
DNA replication; the central dogma; the genetic code

sections.title: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
DNA replication; the central dogma; the genetic code

summary: Griffith showed that a heat-killed virulent pneumococcus could transform a live avirulent one; Avery's group proved with DNase that the principle is DNA; Hershey and Chase proved with ³²P and ³⁵S that DNA, not protein, enters the bacterium.
A nucleotide is phosphate + pentose + base; purines (A, G) have two rings and pyrimidines (C, T, U) one; nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds into a 5′ → 3′ chain.

The Watson–Crick helix is right-handed and antiparallel, 2 nm wide, 3.4 nm per turn, 10 bp per turn and 0.34 nm per base pair, with A=T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds) — so GC-rich DNA is more stable.
Chargaff: A = T, G = C, so purines = pyrimidines; one given percentage fixes the other three.
mRNA carries codons, tRNA is the cloverleaf adaptor with an anticodon and a CCA-3′ amino-acid end, and rRNA is the most abundant RNA and the catalyst that forms peptide bonds.
Replication is semi-conservative: Meselson and Stahl's ¹⁵N experiment gave one hybrid band after one division and equal hybrid and light bands after two.

Helicase unwinds, primase primes, DNA polymerase III extends 5′ → 3′, DNA polymerase I replaces the primer and ligase seals the nicks; the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is a series of Okazaki fragments.
Transcription copies one gene with RNA polymerase and needs no primer; the central dogma is DNA → RNA → protein, with reverse transcription as the exception.

sections.title: Mendelian terminology and laws; incomplete dominance and co-dominance

Gene and chromosomal mutations; polyploidy
Down's, Turner's, Edwards' and Klinefelter's syndromes; albinism; haemophilia

summary: Mendel's pea crosses gave genetics its language (allele, dominant, genotype) and its first two laws: dominance, and segregation — alleles part into gametes unaltered, which meiosis I explains physically.
The signature ratios flow from gamete combinations: 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 in F₂, and test-cross ratios that print out the gametes of the heterozygote directly.
Incomplete dominance (pink Mirabilis, 1 : 2 : 1) and co-dominance (AB blood group) modify expression, never segregation — pure types reappear in F₂.
Genes on one chromosome are linked; their recombination frequency (test-cross minority classes) measures distance in centimorgans, capped at 50%.
Sex-linked recessives (colour blindness, haemophilia, white eye in Drosophila) hit hemizygous males, travel criss-cross through carrier females, and betray themselves by unequal reciprocal crosses.
Mutations change bases (substitutions, frameshifts), chromosome structure, or chromosome number; non-disjunction produces the aneuploid syndromes.
Polyploidy multiplies whole sets: triploids are sterile (seedless fruit), doubled hybrids are fertile new species (bread wheat, Triticale).

Count the karyotype to name the syndrome: 45,XO Turner (female), 47,XXY Klinefelter (male), +21 Down, +18 Edwards; albinism is autosomal recessive (no tyrosinase), haemophilia X-linked recessive (no factor VIII).

topics: Plant tissues: characters, classification, structure and functions
Types of vascular bundles
T.S. of monocot and dicot root, stem and leaf

sections.title: Plant tissues: characters, classification, structure and functions
Types of vascular bundles
T.S. of monocot and dicot root, stem and leaf

summary: Tissues are meristematic (still dividing: apical, intercalary and lateral; primary and, by dedifferentiation, secondary) or permanent (simple and complex).

Parenchyma packs and stores (aerenchyma in hydrophytes), living pectin-rich collenchyma supports growing organs flexibly, and dead lignified sclerenchyma (fibres and stone cells) supports finished ones rigidly.
Xylem moves water up through dead tracheids and vessels, its parenchyma alone alive; phloem moves food through enucleate sieve tubes serviced by companion cells, with bast fibres for strength.

Bundle names encode geometry: radial in roots; collateral and bicollateral conjoint bundles in stems; concentric amphivasal (xylem out) and amphicribral (phloem out); open bundles carry cambium, closed do not.

Roots show epiblema with hairs, a Casparian-striped endodermis with passage cells, pericycle that births lateral roots, and exarch radial groups — few and pith-less in dicots, polyarch with a big pith in monocots.
Dicot stems ring their open bundles round a pith (ready for secondary growth); monocot stems scatter closed, sheathed bundles with a lysigenous cavity through undifferentiated ground tissue.

Dorsiventral dicot leaves split mesophyll into palisade and spongy layers and hide stomata below; isobilateral grass leaves keep mesophyll uniform, bear stomata and dumb-bell guard cells on both faces, and roll up by their bulliform cells.

units.title: Water Relations of Plants
topics: Diffusion, diffusion pressure deficit, osmosis and plasmolysis
Osmotic pressure and potential, water potential, wall pressure and turgor pressure
Absorption, imbibition, ascent of sap, transpiration, guttation and wilting

sections.title: Diffusion, diffusion pressure deficit, osmosis and plasmolysis
Osmotic pressure and potential, water potential, wall pressure and turgor pressure
Absorption, imbibition, ascent of sap, transpiration, guttation and wilting

summary: Diffusion needs no membrane; osmosis is water diffusing across a selectively permeable one; plasmolysis (reversible) demonstrates both the membrane's selectivity and the cell sap's osmotic strength.
Water potential Ψw = Ψs + Ψp rules every movement: pure water is zero, all else negative, and water runs from less negative to more negative; van't Hoff's Ψs = −imRT sizes any solution.
The older DPD = OP − TP is the same physics with flipped signs (Ψw = −DPD): fully turgid means DPD zero; flaccid means DPD = OP.
Roots absorb through root hairs by apoplast, symplast and aquaporin routes, with the Casparian strip as the membrane checkpoint; imbibition by colloids (protein strongest) starts germination.

Root pressure (≈0.1–0.2 MPa) is too feeble and too nocturnal to lift sap; the sun does it instead — transpiration tension dragging a cohesive, adhesive water column from soil to air (Dixon and Joly), with xylem under negative pressure.
Transpiration is mostly stomatal, opened by potassium influx and closed by ABA, driven by vapour pressure deficit and measured with a potometer.

Liquid water forced out of hydathodes by root pressure is guttation (not dew, not bleeding), and loss of turgor shows as wilting — temporary at midday, permanent below the soil's wilting point of about −1.5 MPa.

topics: Photosynthetic pigments; photosystems I and II; the light reactions
Calvin cycle (C3), Hatch–Slack pathway (C4) and photorespiration; factors; bacterial photosynthesis

sections.title: Photosynthetic pigments; photosystems I and II; the light reactions
Calvin cycle (C3), Hatch–Slack pathway (C4) and photorespiration; factors; bacterial photosynthesis
Aerobic and anaerobic respiration: glycolysis, oxidative decarboxylation, Krebs cycle, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation; factors

summary: Chlorophyll a (Mg-centred) alone converts light energy; accessory pigments widen the catch and protect the reaction centres P680 (PS II, acting first) and P700 (PS I).

The Z-scheme drags electrons from water (photolysis at the Mn₄CaO₅ complex, O₂ and protons into the lumen) to NADP⁺, minting ATP chemiosmotically on the way; cyclic flow around PS I adds ATP only, balancing the 3 : 2 budget.
The stromal Calvin cycle carboxylates RuBP via RuBisCO into 3-PGA and, at 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂, builds glucose for 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.

Photorespiration — RuBisCO fixing O₂ — wastes carbon through a three-organelle salvage loop; C4 plants suppress it spatially (Kranz anatomy, PEP carboxylase pump, 5 ATP per CO₂) and CAM plants temporally.

Blackman's limiting-factor law and the two compensation points govern how light, CO₂ (now 0.043%), temperature and water set the photosynthetic rate; bacteria photosynthesise with H₂S and release no O₂.
Glycolysis (cytoplasm) nets 2 ATP + 2 NADH; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (matrix) strip the six carbons out as CO₂, loading 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ in all.
The cristae electron-transport chain, ending at oxygen, converts those carriers into most of the modern 30–32 ATP per glucose (38 classically).
Without oxygen, fermentation merely regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis's 2 ATP (Pasteur effect), and the RQ — 1.0, 0.7, 0.82, above 1 — reports the substrate being burned.

topics: Auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins: roles and applications
Seed germination and its types; seed dormancy

sections.title: Auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins: roles and applications
Seed germination and its types; seed dormancy

summary: Auxin (IAA) was hunted down through the Darwin–Boysen-Jensen–Paál–Went experiments; it elongates cells, enforces apical dominance, roots cuttings and, as 2,4-D, selectively kills dicot weeds — always with a bell-shaped, tissue-specific dose response.
Gibberellins, discovered through the bakanae fungus, elongate internodes (curing genetic dwarfs), bolt rosettes, break dormancy and order the aleurone to make α-amylase.

Cytokinins (kinetin, then natural zeatin from maize) drive cell division with auxin, free lateral buds, and delay senescence; the auxin : cytokinin ratio steers tissue culture between roots, shoots and callus.
Germination begins with imbibition, is powered by aerobic respiration, and is fed when embryo gibberellin switches on the aleurone; the radicle leads the way out.
Hypocotyl growth lifts the cotyledons in epigeal species (bean, castor), epicotyl growth leaves them buried in hypogeal ones (pea, maize), and mangroves skip the wait by vivipary.

Dormant seeds refuse even perfect conditions because of impermeable coats, unfinished embryos or ABA-based inhibition; scarification, stratification, light, gibberellin and leaching remove the blocks nature uses to time germination.

summary: Plants clone themselves by rhizomes, tubers, bulbs, runners, leaf buds and even apomictic seed — fast and faithful, but variation-free; growers exploit the same tricks by cutting, layering and grafting.

The anther's tapetum feeds microspores produced four-at-a-time by PMC meiosis; each becomes a sporopollenin-armoured pollen grain carrying a tube cell and a generative cell (source of the two gametes).
The ovule's single functional megaspore builds, by three mitoses, the 7-celled, 8-nucleate Polygonum embryo sac — egg apparatus, central cell with two polar nuclei, three antipodals.

Pollination spans autogamy to xenogamy on wind, water, insects, birds and bats, with cleistogamy guaranteeing selfing and dicliny, dichogamy, herkogamy, heterostyly and self-incompatibility enforcing crossing.
Double fertilization — syngamy making the 2n zygote, triple fusion the 3n endosperm — is unique to angiosperms and economical: food tissue is made only when an embryo exists.
The dicot embryo (suspensor, two cotyledons, terminal plumule) contrasts with the monocot's scutellum, coleoptile and coleorhiza.

Endosperm develops by nuclear, cellular or helobial patterns and may persist (albuminous seeds, with aleurone in cereals) or be absorbed into the cotyledons (exalbuminous); perisperm is persistent 2n nucellus, not endosperm.

Genetic engineering: concept and applications

sections.title: Plant tissue culture: concept, types and applications

Biofertilizers, green manures, plant breeding, bio-engineering, food safety and security

summary: Tissue culture milks totipotency on MS medium: sterilised explants pass through callus to shoots (cytokinin) and roots (auxin), then hardening — the engine of micropropagation and the finishing step of all plant genetic engineering.

Specialised cultures earn their keep: meristems for virus-free stock, anthers for haploids and instant pure lines, rescued embryos for wide crosses, fused protoplasts for somatic hybrids, liquid nitrogen for germplasm.

Genetic engineering cuts with restriction enzymes, glues with ligase, ferries genes on plasmid or Ti vectors, selects on markers, and amplifies DNA with PCR; its products range from Humulin and Flavr Savr to Bt crops and Golden Rice, under Cartagena-style biosafety rules (and no registered GM cultivation in Nepal).

Plant breeding improves crops by introduction, selection, hybridisation, mutation and polyploidy — trading variation for uniformity carefully, using backcrosses for single resistance genes and heterosis for yield.
Biofertilizers inoculate the soil with nitrogen fixers, phosphate solubilisers and mycorrhiza; green manures sacrifice a legume crop to feed the next one.

Bio-engineering runs biology at industrial scale — fermenters, biogas, bioremediation — while food safety (hazard control: HACCP, DFTQC) and food security (FAO's four pillars of access) frame why all of it matters.
